group.title: More idioms
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To avoid saying something directly.
examples: Stop {beating around the bush} and tell me.
wrong: She beat around the bush by saying it directly.

words.meaning: A very small amount compared to what is needed.
examples: The donation is {a drop in the ocean}.
wrong: A million dollars for one coffee is a drop in the ocean.

words.meaning: Back to the beginning after a failed attempt.
examples: The plan failed, so we’re {back to square one}.
wrong: We finished it perfectly, so we’re back to square one.

words.lemma: bite off more than you can chew
words.meaning: To take on more than you can manage.
examples: I {bit off more than I could chew} with three jobs.
wrong: He bit off more than he could chew, so the work was easy.
words.ipa: /ˌbaɪt ˈɔf ˈmɔr ðən ju kən ˈtʃu/

words.meaning: To work or study late at night.
examples: She {burned the midnight oil} before the exam.
wrong: I burned the midnight oil, so I went to bed at eight.

words.lemma: by the skin of your teeth
words.meaning: Only just; by a very small margin.
examples: He passed {by the skin of his teeth}.
wrong: She won by the skin of her teeth, by a huge margin.

words.lemma: cost an arm and a leg
words.meaning: To be very expensive.
examples: That car must {cost an arm and a leg}.
wrong: The coffee cost an arm and a leg: just one cent.

words.meaning: To be upset about something that can’t be changed.
examples: It’s done; don’t {cry over spilt milk}.
wrong: The vase is broken; let’s cry over spilt milk and glue it back so it looks new.

words.meaning: To become nervous and decide not to do something.
examples: He {got cold feet} before the wedding.
wrong: She got cold feet, so she went ahead happily.

words.meaning: To start an activity.
examples: Let’s {get the ball rolling} with introductions.
wrong: We got the ball rolling by ending the meeting.

words.meaning: To make more effort than is expected.
examples: She always {goes the extra mile} for customers.
wrong: He went the extra mile by doing as little as possible.

words.lemma: hit the nail on the head
words.meaning: To describe something exactly right.
examples: You {hit the nail on the head} with that point.
wrong: She hit the nail on the head, so her answer was wrong.

words.meaning: In trouble.
examples: He’s {in hot water} for missing the deadline.
wrong: She’s in hot water, so her boss is very pleased.

words.meaning: To join something because it is popular.
examples: Many firms {jumped on the bandwagon} of AI.
wrong: He jumped on the bandwagon by doing what nobody else did.

words.meaning: To avoid talking about an old problem.
examples: I decided to {let sleeping dogs lie}.
wrong: I let sleeping dogs lie by bringing up the old fight again.

words.meaning: To lose a chance by being too slow.
examples: If you don’t apply now, you’ll {miss the boat}.
wrong: I missed the boat, so I got the chance I wanted.

words.meaning: In a risky situation.
examples: After two warnings, he’s {on thin ice}.
wrong: He’s on thin ice, so his job is perfectly safe.

words.meaning: To argue the opposite view to test an idea.
examples: Let me {play devil’s advocate} for a minute.
wrong: She played devil’s advocate by agreeing with everyone in the room.

words.meaning: To do your fair share of work.
examples: Everyone must {pull their weight}.
wrong: He pulled his weight by letting others do his work.

words.meaning: To understand a hidden meaning.
examples: If you {read between the lines}, he’s unhappy.
wrong: I read between the lines, so I only understood the exact words.

words.meaning: To agree with someone.
examples: We don’t always {see eye to eye}.
wrong: We see eye to eye, so we disagree on everything.

words.meaning: To avoid choosing a side.
examples: Stop {sitting on the fence} and decide.
wrong: She sat on the fence by choosing a side clearly.

words.meaning: To take attention or praise from someone else.
examples: His announcement {stole her thunder}.
wrong: He stole her thunder by praising her success in front of everyone.

words.meaning: With doubt; not believing something completely.
examples: Take his stories {with a pinch of salt}.
wrong: I took the news with a pinch of salt, so I believed every word.

words.lemma: the ball is in your court
words.meaning: It is your turn to decide or act.
examples: I’ve made my offer; {the ball is in your court}.
wrong: The ball is in your court, so I have to decide what we do next.

words.meaning: To give up.
examples: After ten defeats, he {threw in the towel}.
wrong: She threw in the towel and kept going for years.

words.meaning: To pretend not to notice something wrong.
examples: The manager {turned a blind eye} to the late arrivals.
wrong: He turned a blind eye by reporting every case.

words.meaning: Never; used to say something will not happen.
examples: He’ll apologize {when pigs fly}.
wrong: He’ll arrive when pigs fly, probably at six o’clock tonight.

words.meaning: To make a bad situation worse.
examples: To {add insult to injury}, it started to rain.
wrong: To add insult to injury, the sun came out and the day got better.

words.meaning: The advantages of two different things at once.
examples: Working from home gives me {the best of both worlds}.
wrong: The job is boring and badly paid; it’s the best of both worlds.

words.meaning: To be the person who makes decisions.
examples: In this office, she {calls the shots}.
wrong: He calls the shots, so he never decides anything.

words.meaning: To get to the main point without wasting time.
examples: Let’s {cut to the chase}: how much?
wrong: He cut to the chase by talking about the weather for an hour.

words.meaning: An obvious problem that nobody talks about.
examples: Money was {the elephant in the room}.
wrong: The elephant in the room was the topic everyone discussed openly.

words.meaning: To accept punishment for what you did.
examples: He finally had to {face the music}.
wrong: She faced the music by running away.

words.meaning: To become impossible to control.
examples: The party {got out of hand}.
wrong: Things got out of hand, so everything stayed calm.

words.meaning: To start something with energy and speed.
examples: The new manager {hit the ground running}.
wrong: She hit the ground running by waiting a month to start.

words.meaning: To learn how to do a job.
examples: It took a month to {learn the ropes}.
wrong: After twenty years in the job, she was still learning the ropes on her first day.

words.meaning: To change the rules unfairly.
examples: Just as we finished, they {moved the goalposts}.
wrong: They moved the goalposts by keeping every rule exactly the same.

words.meaning: To stop a problem early.
examples: If you see bullying, {nip it in the bud}.
wrong: We nipped it in the bud by letting it grow for years.

words.meaning: Time to start planning again after failure.
examples: The test failed, so it’s {back to the drawing board}.
wrong: The plan worked perfectly, so it’s back to the drawing board.

words.meaning: To think in a new and creative way.
examples: We need to {think outside the box}.
wrong: He thought outside the box by copying the usual plan exactly.

words.meaning: Something very easy.
examples: The exam was {a piece of cake}.
wrong: The test was a piece of cake, so nobody passed.

words.meaning: Without being noticed.
examples: The deal went {under the radar}.
wrong: The scandal went under the radar, on every front page.

words.meaning: A small visible part of a much bigger problem.
examples: These complaints are just {the tip of the iceberg}.
wrong: These five complaints are the tip of the iceberg; there are no others.

words.meaning: To do something that has not been done before.
examples: The study {broke new ground} in medicine.
wrong: The study broke new ground by repeating an old experiment exactly.
